title: Files, Folders & Permissions
sub: Navigate the macOS filesystem, move and find things, archive and verify them, and control who can touch what
goals: Explain what lives where on a Mac and read any absolute or relative path
Create, copy, move, link and delete files and folders without losing data
Find files by name, type, size and age with find, mdfind and zsh globs
Archive, compress and checksum a folder and verify the copy
Read ls -l and set permissions with chmod, in symbolic and octal form
Recover from Permission denied and Operation not permitted by diagnosing the cause

blocks.text: Everything on a Unix system is reachable as a path in one tree, and almost every command you will run in this book takes a path or produces one. In this chapter you will learn the layout of the macOS tree, how paths work, the commands that create, move, inspect, find, pack and protect files, and the permission model that decides who may read, write or run each one. You will also meet the extra layers macOS adds on top of classic Unix: extended attributes, quarantine, ACLs, System Integrity Protection and privacy permissions.

The examples use `~/lab` from [Setting up your lab](#setup). Destructive experiments happen in scratch copies: run `cp -R ~/lab/data ~/lab/data-work` when an exercise tells you to change files, and keep `~/lab/data` pristine for later chapters.
The macOS filesystem layout
macOS has one tree rooted at `/`. Its layout is a mix of classic Unix directories, Apple's own, and Homebrew's. These are the ones you will touch:

blocks.code:
/
  ├── ⟪c:Users⟫/learner/          your home: Desktop, Documents, Downloads, lab, .zshrc, .ssh
  ├── ⟪c:Applications⟫/           apps for all users (Safari.app, PyCharm.app ...)
  ├── ⟪c:Library⟫/                system-wide support files, preferences, launch daemons
  ├── ⟪d:System⟫/                 the operating system itself (read-only, sealed)
  ├── ⟪g:usr⟫/
  │    ├── bin, sbin            system commands (ls, grep, ping ...) - do not modify
  │    ├── lib, libexec, share  libraries and data for those commands
  │    └── local/               traditional place for software you installed (Intel Homebrew uses it)
  ├── ⟪g:opt⟫/homebrew/           Homebrew on Apple Silicon: bin, Cellar, etc
  ├── bin, sbin                 more essential commands (sh, zsh, cp, mv ...)
  ├── ⟪y:private⟫/                real home of etc, var and tmp
  │    ├── etc                  system config: hosts, ssh, zshrc    (/etc is a symlink here)
  │    ├── var                  logs, caches, databases             (/var is a symlink here)
  │    └── tmp                  temporary files                     (/tmp is a symlink here)
  ├── ⟪m:Volumes⟫/                mount points: external drives, disk images, network shares
  └── dev                       device files: /dev/null, /dev/tty ...

head: Directory
What it holds
Notes
rows: each person's files; `~` is a shortcut to your own
the only place you normally write
each `.app` is really a folder (a bundle)
settings and support files shared by all users
distinct from `~/Library`, which is per user and hidden in Finder
on a separate, read-only, cryptographically sealed volume; even `sudo` cannot change it
protected by SIP; `ls`, `cat` and `grep` live here
Intel Homebrew prefix; empty or partial on Apple Silicon
your startup disk also appears here as a link

blocks.text: Since macOS 10.15 the startup disk is split into a read-only **System** volume and a read-write **Data** volume (named like "Macintosh HD - Data"). Firmlinks stitch them into one tree so you do not see the seam. Your files live on the Data volume, and macOS updates replace the System volume without touching them. `/etc`, `/tmp` and `/var` are symbolic links into `/private`, so `ls -ld /tmp` shows a link, while paths printed by tools often appear as `/private/tmp/...`.
Paths
A **path** names a location. Two forms:

items.text: **Absolute**: starts with `/` and means the same thing everywhere: `/Users/learner/lab/access.log`.
**Relative**: does not start with `/` and is interpreted from the **current working directory**: `data/alpha.txt`.

blocks.text: Special names work in any path:

head: Name
Means
Example
rows: `./script.zsh` runs a file in the current folder (the shell does not search `.` for programs)
your home directory (expanded by the shell)
the root, or a separator between components

blocks.text: Names that begin with `.` are **hidden**: globs skip them and `ls` omits them unless you add `-a`. Finder hides them too (press [[Cmd+Shift+.]] to toggle). Config files like `.zshrc`, `.ssh` and `.git` are hidden by convention.

macOS file names may contain spaces, which split into separate words unless you quote: `cd "My Documents"` or `cd My\ Documents`. The default APFS volume is **case-insensitive but case-preserving**: `Notes.txt` and `notes.txt` are the same file here, though not on Linux or in a case-sensitive volume, so a script that works on your Mac can fail on a server.
Three small tools take paths apart and normalize them:

zsh also has **history-style modifiers on variables**: with `f=~/lab/data/../access.log`, `${f:A}` gives the absolute, symlink-resolved path (`/Users/learner/lab/access.log`), `${f:t}` the tail (file name), `${f:h}` the head (directory), `${f:r}` the name without its extension, and `${f:e}` the extension only.

blocks.name: pwd
blocks.sum: Print the absolute path of the current working directory.

how.text: The shell tracks a current directory for itself and for every program it starts, and relative paths are resolved against it. `pwd` prints it. By default it shows the logical path you navigated through; `-P` resolves symbolic links and prints the physical path, which is how `/tmp` becomes `/private/tmp`.

flags.d: Print the physical path with symbolic links resolved.

examples.desc: Where am I?
Copy the current path to the clipboard
Name of the current folder only

blocks.name: cd
blocks.sum: Change the shell's current working directory.

how.text: `cd` is a builtin, not a program, because a child process cannot change its parent's directory. With no argument it goes to `$HOME`, with `-` to the previous directory (in `$OLDPWD`). zsh adds conveniences: `setopt AUTO_CD` lets you type a directory name alone, `cd old new` replaces `old` with `new` in the current path, and `setopt CDABLE_VARS` lets you `cd` to a variable's value.

examples.desc: Go into the lab and back
Go to the folder that contains a file
Jump to the newest subdirectory

gotchas: A path with spaces needs quotes. `cd` into a file or a missing path fails with `not a directory` or `no such file or directory` and leaves you where you were.

blocks.name: ls
blocks.sum: List directory contents and file metadata.

how.text: `ls` reads a directory and prints names, sorted alphabetically unless you say otherwise. With a file argument it lists just that file, and with `-d` it lists a directory itself instead of its contents. `-l` switches to long format with permissions, owner, size and date (read it with the anatomy below). On macOS this is BSD `ls`: `-G` colors output (or set `CLICOLOR=1`), there is no `--color` or `--sort`, `-h` prints human sizes, `-O` shows file flags such as `hidden` or `restricted`, `-@` lists extended attributes, and `-e` shows ACLs.

flags.d: Long format: permissions, links, owner, group, size, date, name.
Include hidden files (`.` and `..` too); `-A` leaves out `.` and `..`.
Sort by modification time, newest first; `-r` reverses any sort.
List directories themselves, not their contents.
One entry per line (what you get automatically when piping).

examples.desc: Everything, long, human sizes, newest last
Is this directory's permission what I think?
The three biggest files in this folder
Count entries
Names of the files changed most recently

gotchas: Never parse `ls` output for scripting with file names that might contain spaces or newlines. Use globs (`for f in *.log`) or `find -print0`.

blocks.code:
$ cd ~/lab
$ ls -lS | head -4
total 88
-rw-r--r--  1 learner  staff  13163 Sep 14 10:22 access.log
-rw-r--r--  1 learner  staff   1153 Sep 14 10:22 scan.txt
-rw-r--r--  1 learner  staff    798 Sep 14 10:22 ping.log
$ ls -lhS data
total 40
-rw-r--r--  1 learner  staff  155B Sep 14 10:22 gamma.log

-rw-r--r--  1 learner  staff   68B Sep 14 10:22 report-2026-09.csv

blocks.text: Every column of `ls -l` carries a fact. Read them left to right:

tokens.exp: first character is the type (- file, d directory, l link); then three triples r/w/x for owner, group, others; @ means extended attributes, + means an ACL
number of hard links to this file
modification time (older than six months shows a year instead of the time)

blocks.name: mkdir
blocks.sum: Create one or more directories.

how.text: `mkdir name` creates a directory in the current location. Without `-p` the parent must already exist and the command fails if the directory exists. `-p` creates all missing parents and is silent if the directory is already there, which makes it safe to repeat in scripts. Zsh brace expansion builds whole trees in one command.

flags.d: Create parents as needed; no error if it exists.
Print each directory as it is created.

examples.desc: A project skeleton in one command
Make a dated folder

blocks.name: rmdir
blocks.sum: Remove empty directories.

how.text: `rmdir` deletes a directory only if it is **empty**, which makes it a safe way to remove a folder: it cannot take any files with it. `-p` also removes empty parents.

examples.desc: Remove an empty folder
Remove every empty directory below a path

gotchas: `rmdir: Directory not empty` is the command doing its job. Hidden files such as `.DS_Store` count as content; see with `ls -A`.

blocks.name: touch
blocks.sum: Create an empty file, or update an existing file's timestamps.

how.text: If the file does not exist, `touch` creates it empty. If it does, `touch` sets its modification time to now without changing its contents. `-t` sets a specific time and `-r` copies the times from another file. Build tools and backups use timestamps, so `touch` is also a way to mark a point in time.

flags.d: Use this time instead of now, in `YYYYMMDDhhmm` form.

examples.desc: Create three empty files
Backdate a file by choosing a time
Create files named after each host in hosts.txt

blocks.name: cp
blocks.sum: Copy files and directories.

how.text: `cp source dest` writes a new file with the same contents; the copy gets the new timestamp and your default permissions unless you ask to preserve them. Copying a directory requires `-R` (recursive). When the destination is an existing directory, the source is copied into it. On macOS `-a` is archive mode (recursive, preserve permissions, times and symlinks), `-c` makes an instant copy-on-write clone on APFS, and `-n` refuses to overwrite.

flags.d: Archive: `-R` plus preserve permissions, times, symlinks.
Clone using APFS copy-on-write (instant, no extra space until changed).

examples.desc: Back up a file with a dated name
Copy a folder safely into a scratch area
Copy only the .log files from a list

gotchas: Without `-n` or `-i`, `cp` overwrites silently. Trailing slashes on a source directory behave differently between BSD (macOS) and GNU (Linux) `cp`; for exact, metadata-preserving copies use `ditto` or `rsync`.

blocks.name: mv
blocks.sum: Move or rename files and directories.

how.text: Renaming and moving are the same operation: changing the name (path) that points at the data. Within one volume `mv` is instant whatever the size, because only the directory entry changes. Across volumes it copies then deletes. If the destination is an existing file it is **replaced without warning**, unless you use `-i` or `-n`.

examples.desc: Rename a file
Move all logs into a folder
Rename every .txt to .md (zsh's zmv does this more elegantly, but this works anywhere)
examples.code: for f in *.txt(N); do mv -- "$f" "${f%.txt}.md"; done

gotchas: `mv file dir` when `dir` does not exist renames `file` to `dir`. Add a trailing slash (`mv file dir/`) so a missing directory is an error instead.

blocks.name: rm
blocks.sum: Remove files; with -r, remove directories and everything in them.

how.text: `rm` unlinks names from the filesystem. There is **no Trash and no undelete**: on an SSD with APFS, deleted data is effectively gone, snapshots aside. `rm file` refuses directories; `-r` recurses; `-d` removes an empty directory; `-f` suppresses all questions and errors; `-i` asks before each removal and `-I` asks once before removing many files.

flags.d: One prompt before removing more than three files or recursing.
Force: no prompts, ignore missing files.

examples.desc: Remove one file, asking first
Look first, then remove
Delete files older than 30 days, after reviewing the list

gotchas: `rm -rf` with a variable that is empty or has a space (`rm -rf $dir/ *`) can wipe your home folder. Quote variables, never run it with `sudo` out of habit, and run the matching `ls` first.

blocks.text: `rm -rf path` deletes a whole tree without asking and without the Trash. The classic disasters are a stray space (`rm -rf ~/ lab`), an empty variable (`rm -rf "$DIR"/*`) and a glob that matches more than you expected. Build the habit: **run `ls` with the exact same arguments first**, read the list, then recall the line with the up arrow and change `ls` to `rm`. When learning, use `rm -i` or `mv file ~/.Trash/` instead. Try destructive commands in a scratch folder, never in your home folder.

blocks.name: ln
blocks.sum: Create a hard link or, with -s, a symbolic link (shortcut) to a file or directory.

how.text: A **hard link** is a second name for the same data (the same inode); deleting one name leaves the other. It cannot cross volumes or point to directories. A **symbolic link** is a small file that stores a path; it can point anywhere, even to something that does not exist (a dangling link). Most of the time you want `-s`. The order is `ln -s WHERE_IT_POINTS NAME_OF_THE_LINK`, the reverse of what feels natural.

flags.d: Replace an existing link or file.
Treat an existing symlink to a directory as a file (use with `-f` to replace it).

examples.desc: Put your scripts on the PATH via a link
List all symlinks in a folder and where they point

gotchas: A relative link target is resolved from the **link's** directory, not from where you ran `ln`. Use absolute targets while learning.

blocks.text: Looking inside files

blocks.name: cat
blocks.sum: Print files to standard output, or concatenate several into one stream.

how.text: `cat` reads each file in order and writes it to stdout; with no arguments it copies stdin. It is mostly used to feed a file into a pipeline or to join files (`cat a b > c`). On a large file use `less` instead. `-n` numbers lines, `-s` squeezes repeated blank lines, and `-et` makes line ends (`$`) and tabs (`^I`) visible, which diagnoses stray whitespace and Windows `^M` line endings.

flags.d: Squeeze multiple blank lines into one.
Show `$` at the end of each line (and non-printing characters).

examples.desc: Number the lines of a file
Check for hidden whitespace
Join all logs in a folder into one stream and count the lines

gotchas: `cat file | cmd` is fine for readability, but `cmd < file` avoids one process, and `cat file > file` truncates the input first.

blocks.code:
$ cd ~/lab
$ cat -n notes.txt | head -3
     1	Lab notebook
     2	============
     3	TODO: replace the old router password
$ head -n 2 hosts.txt
example.com
python.org
$ tail -n 2 hosts.txt
openbsd.org
iana.org
$ tail -n +9 hosts.txt
openbsd.org
iana.org

blocks.name: less
blocks.sum: Page through a file or a command's output, with search and backward scrolling.

how.text: `less` shows one screenful at a time and does not load the whole file, so it opens huge logs instantly. It is the pager behind `man` and `git log`. Keys: **Space** or **f** forward a page, **b** back, **j**/**k** or the arrows by line, **g** top, **G** bottom, **/text** search forward (**n** next, **N** previous), **?text** search backward, **&pattern** show only matching lines, **q** quit. `-S` stops long lines wrapping (scroll sideways with the arrow keys), `-N` numbers lines, `-R` passes ANSI colors, and `+F` starts in follow mode like `tail -f` (press [[Ctrl+C]] to stop following, `F` to resume).

flags.d: Chop long lines instead of wrapping.
Pass colors through (use with `ls -G` or colored `grep` output).

examples.desc: Browse the log with line numbers
Page a long listing without wrapping
Page colored grep output

blocks.name: more
blocks.sum: An older pager; on macOS it runs `less` in a compatible mode.

how.text: `more` shows a file a page at a time. On macOS it is a compatibility front end to `less`, so the same keys work. Prefer typing `less`. You will meet `more` in old tutorials and in some scripts.

examples.desc: Page a file

blocks.name: head
blocks.sum: Print the first lines (or bytes) of a file.

how.text: `head` prints the first 10 lines by default. It stops reading as soon as it has enough, so `command | head` ends the upstream program early (it gets SIGPIPE). BSD `head` on macOS does **not** accept a negative count such as `head -n -3` to mean "all but the last three"; use `sed '$d'` or `awk` for that.

examples.desc: First five lines
The three most recent log files, listed
Peek at the header row of a CSV

gotchas: With several files, `head` prints a `==> name <==` banner before each.

blocks.name: tail
blocks.sum: Print the last lines of a file, or follow it as it grows.

how.text: `tail` prints the last 10 lines. `tail -n +2` means "start at line 2", which skips a header row. `-f` follows: it keeps the file open and prints new lines as they are appended, which is how you watch a live log. `-F` also copes with the file being replaced (log rotation). Follow mode never ends by itself; stop it with [[Ctrl+C]].

flags.d: Last N lines; `-n +N` starts at line N.
Follow, and reopen the file if it is renamed or recreated.
Reverse: print lines in reverse order (BSD).

examples.desc: Watch a log being written
Skip the CSV header
Watch only errors as they arrive
Last line of each log in a folder
examples.code: for f in data/*.log; do echo "$f: $(tail -n 1 $f)"; done

blocks.name: file
blocks.sum: Tell you what kind of data a file contains, by looking at its content rather than its name.

how.text: `file` reads the start of each file and compares it with a database of signatures ("magic numbers"), so it recognizes an image renamed to `.txt` or a script without an extension. `-b` omits the file name from the output and `-I` prints the MIME type (`text/plain; charset=us-ascii`).

flags.d: Brief: do not print the file name.

examples.desc: Identify a file
Find which files in a folder are really shell scripts
Find the compiled (Mach-O) programs in /usr/bin

blocks.name: stat
blocks.sum: Print every piece of metadata the filesystem stores about a file.

how.text: `stat` shows inode, permissions, links, owner, size and the access, modify, change and birth times. BSD `stat` on macOS uses `-f` with `%` codes (GNU `stat` uses `-c`, a common source of errors when copying Linux commands). `-x` prints a Linux-style multi-line form. Useful codes: `%z` size in bytes, `%N` name, `%Sp` permissions as text, `%Lp` permissions in octal, `%Su` owner, `%Sg` group, `%Sm` modification time (formatted with `-t`), `%a` access time.

examples.desc: Octal permissions and name
Size, owner and modification time
Show permissions of every file in a folder in octal
Find the file with the largest size

gotchas: `stat -c '%a %n' file` is the GNU spelling and fails on macOS with `illegal option -- c`.

blocks.text: Size and space

blocks.name: du
blocks.sum: Report how much disk space files and directories use.

how.text: `du` adds up the disk blocks used under each path, recursively. `-s` prints one summary per argument instead of a line per subdirectory, `-h` prints human-readable sizes, `-d N` limits the depth of the report (BSD uses `-d`; GNU's `--max-depth` does not exist on macOS), and `-c` adds a grand total. Pipe to `sort -h` to rank.

flags.d: Report only to N levels deep.
Report in 1 KB blocks (stable output for scripts).

examples.desc: How big is each item here?
The five largest items in a folder
Largest folders, human sizes, two levels deep

gotchas: `du` counts blocks allocated, so a 1-byte file shows 4 KB. And with APFS clones and snapshots, `du` and Finder can disagree.

blocks.name: df
blocks.sum: Show free and used space on each mounted filesystem.

how.text: `df` asks each mounted filesystem for its totals. `-h` prints human units, and giving a path (`df -h .`) shows only the filesystem containing it. On an APFS Mac several volumes share one container, so the numbers for `/` and for the Data volume overlap; the figure that matters for "how much can I still store" is the **Avail** column of the Data volume (mounted at `/System/Volumes/Data`).

examples.desc: Space on the volume that holds this folder
Just the percent used for the data volume

blocks.name: tree
blocks.sum: Draw a directory as an indented tree.

how.text: Install with `brew install tree`. `tree` walks a directory and prints it as a tree, which is the quickest way to understand or document a project layout. `-L 2` limits the depth, `-a` includes hidden files, `-d` shows only directories, `-h` shows sizes and `-I 'pattern'` excludes names matching a pattern (use `-I '.git|__pycache__'`).

examples.desc: Two levels of the lab
Capture a project layout for a README

blocks.text: Finding things
You have three ways to find files, each suited to a job:

head: Tool
Searches
Strength
Weakness
rows: short, no extra process, powerful qualifiers
zsh only; huge trees can be slow
portable, precise tests, runs commands on hits
instant across the whole disk, searches content and metadata
only indexed locations; may lag behind recent changes

blocks.name: find
blocks.sum: Walk directory trees and select files by name, type, size, age, permissions and more, optionally running a command on each.

how.text: `find` descends each starting path and evaluates the **expression** on every entry. Tests such as `-name`, `-type`, `-size` and `-mtime` are joined by an implicit AND; `-o` is OR, `!` is NOT and parentheses group (escape them as `\(` and `\)`). The **action** at the end decides what happens: `-print` (the default) prints names, `-exec cmd {} \;` runs `cmd` once per hit, `-exec cmd {} +` batches many names into one call (much faster), `-delete` removes, `-print0` writes NUL-separated names for `xargs -0`. On macOS you must give a path (`find .`). Put `-maxdepth N` before the tests.

flags.d: Name matches the glob (quote it); `-iname` ignores case.
Larger than N; suffixes `k`, `M`, `G` (`-size +10M`); `-size -1k` smaller; `-empty` zero length.
Modified N*24 hours ago: `-mtime -7` within a week, `+30` older than 30 days; `-mmin -60` for minutes.
Do not descend below N levels.
Run CMD on batches of results.
Print names separated by NUL bytes, for `xargs -0`.
Remove each match (dangerous: test with `-print` first).

examples.desc: All log files, any depth
Files larger than 1 MB changed in the last week
Count lines in every log, in batches
Delete old .tmp files safely with spaces in names
The five largest files under a folder
examples.code: find {{dir}} -type f -exec wc -c {} + | grep -v ' total$' | sort -rn | head -5

anat.exp: test: name matches the quoted glob (quote it so the shell does not expand it)
action: run wc -l, with {} replaced by many matched names at a time

gotchas: Unquoted `-name *.log` is expanded by zsh *before* find runs, which either errors (`no matches found`) or passes the wrong names. Always quote the pattern.
`-delete` or `-exec rm` before you have looked at `-print` output is how files vanish. Print first, delete second.

blocks.code:
$ cd ~/lab
$ find . -name '*.log' -type f
./access.log
./data/archive/old.log
./data/delta.log
./data/gamma.log
./ping.log
$ find . -type f -size +1k
./access.log
./scan.txt
$ find . -name '*.log' -exec wc -l {} +
     120 ./access.log
       1 ./data/archive/old.log
       3 ./data/delta.log
       4 ./data/gamma.log
      15 ./ping.log
     143 total
$ find . -type f -exec wc -c {} + | sort -rn | head -4
   17397 total
   13163 ./access.log
    1153 ./scan.txt
     798 ./ping.log

blocks.name: mdfind
blocks.sum: Search the Spotlight index from the command line, by name, content or metadata.

how.text: Spotlight keeps a database of file names, contents and metadata, so `mdfind` finds things instantly even on huge disks. A plain argument searches content and names. `-name` restricts to file names, `-onlyin dir` restricts to a directory and its descendants, and queries can use attributes such as `kMDItemKind == "PDF"` or `kMDItemFSSize > 1000000`. Results can be fed to other commands.

flags.d: Print only the number of matches.

examples.desc: Find files by name in your home folder
Find PDFs by attribute
Open the first result in its default app
Total size of every PDF found
examples.code: mdfind -0 'kMDItemContentType == "com.adobe.pdf"' | xargs -0 stat -f '%z' | awk '{s+=$1} END {print s/1048576, "MB"}'

gotchas: Folders excluded from Spotlight (Privacy list, or `mdutil -i off`) and hidden system folders do not appear. Use `find` when you need certainty.

blocks.name: mdls
blocks.sum: List the Spotlight metadata attributes of a file.

how.text: `mdls` prints the metadata Spotlight stores: content type, kind, creation and modification dates, size, and for media files dimensions, author or duration. `-name` selects one attribute and `-raw` prints its bare value, which makes it script-friendly.

flags.d: Print the value without the attribute name.

examples.desc: Everything known about a file
Just the content type
Which downloaded files came from which site?

blocks.text: Opening, clipboard and path pieces

blocks.name: open
blocks.sum: Open files, folders, URLs and apps as if you had double-clicked them in Finder.

how.text: `open` hands an argument to LaunchServices, which picks the default application. `open .` shows the current folder in Finder, `open -R file` reveals a file in Finder, `open -a "Visual Studio Code" file` picks the app, `-t` uses the default text editor and `-e` uses TextEdit. A URL opens in your browser. It returns immediately and does not wait for the app unless you add `-W`.

flags.d: Reveal in Finder instead of opening.
Open with the default text editor.
Open a new instance of the app.

examples.desc: Show the current folder in Finder
Open a URL
Open every .log file in the default text editor

blocks.name: pbcopy
blocks.sum: Copy standard input to the macOS clipboard.

how.text: `pbcopy` reads stdin and puts it on the system pasteboard, so [[Cmd+V]] pastes it anywhere. It is the end of many pipelines: build a result, send it to the clipboard, paste it into a chat or an editor. It adds nothing, so a trailing newline from `echo` is copied too; use `printf` or `tr -d '\n'` to avoid it.

examples.desc: Copy a file's contents
Copy your IP address

blocks.name: pbpaste
blocks.sum: Write the clipboard's text to standard output.

how.text: `pbpaste` prints whatever text is on the clipboard so a pipeline can process it. Copy a table from a web page, then `pbpaste | awk ...`. Combined with `pbcopy` it transforms the clipboard in place.

examples.desc: Save the clipboard to a file
Sort and de-duplicate the clipboard
Count the lines you copied

blocks.name: basename
blocks.sum: Print the last component of a path, optionally with a suffix removed.

how.text: `basename /a/b/c.txt` prints `c.txt`; with a suffix, `basename /a/b/c.txt .txt` prints `c`. It does not check that the path exists; it only manipulates the text. In zsh the same job is `${path:t}` (tail) and `${path:r}` (remove extension).

examples.desc: Name without extension
Names of all logs without the path

blocks.name: dirname
blocks.sum: Print everything but the last component of a path.

how.text: `dirname /a/b/c.txt` prints `/a/b`. For a bare name it prints `.`. It is the partner of `basename` and is mostly used to find the folder that holds a file or script: `cd "$(dirname "$0")"`. The zsh equivalent is `${path:h}`.

examples.desc: Folder of a file
Unique folders that contain logs

blocks.name: realpath
blocks.sum: Print the absolute, symlink-free form of a path.

how.text: `realpath` resolves `.`, `..` and symbolic links and prints the canonical absolute path. Recent macOS releases include it (check with `type realpath`); `readlink -f` works from macOS 12.3 and `${path:A}` works in any zsh. Resolve a path before comparing two paths or storing one in a config.

examples.desc: Where does this link really point?
The zsh way, which works everywhere zsh does
Resolve every file in a folder

blocks.text: Archives, compression and checksums

An **archive** bundles many files into one (`tar`, `zip`). **Compression** shrinks data (`gzip`). `tar.gz` does both, `zip` does both at once. A **checksum** is a short fingerprint of a file: if even one bit changes, the checksum changes, so comparing checksums proves two copies are identical.

blocks.name: tar
blocks.sum: Create, list and extract archive files, with optional compression.

how.text: One of three actions is required: `-c` create, `-t` list, `-x` extract. `-f archive` names the archive file (it must be followed by the name), and `-z` selects gzip compression. On macOS this is `bsdtar`, which detects the compression automatically when reading, so `tar -xf` works for `.tgz`, `.tar.bz2` and `.tar.xz`. `-C dir` changes to `dir` first. `--exclude pattern` skips files. Always **list before you extract** to avoid unpacking a hundred files into the current folder.

examples.desc: Archive a folder
See what is inside, then extract to a chosen folder
Copy a directory tree through a pipe, preserving structure
Archive only files modified in the last day

anat.exp: the archive file to write (the name must come right after f)
first change into this directory, so paths inside the archive are relative
what to put in the archive

gotchas: macOS tar stores Apple metadata as hidden `._name` entries. Set `COPYFILE_DISABLE=1` in front of the command to leave them out when the archive is for Linux.
Old-style `tar czf out.tgz dir` (no dash) still works, but its options depend on order. Use the dash form and put `-f` last in a bundle (`-czf name`).

blocks.name: zip
blocks.sum: Create a .zip archive; unzip extracts or lists one.
blocks.syntax: zip [-r] [-x pattern] archive.zip file ...      unzip [-l] [-d dir] archive.zip

how.text: `zip -r out.zip folder` zips a directory recursively (`-r` is needed for directories). `-x` excludes patterns. `unzip -l` lists without extracting and `unzip -d dir` extracts into a directory. Zip is the format to use when the recipient is on Windows. `zip -e` adds a password, but zip's classic encryption is weak; use it only to deter casual snooping.

examples.desc: Zip a folder, leaving out Finder clutter
List first, then extract
How many files are in a zip?

blocks.name: gzip
blocks.sum: Compress a single file with gzip, or decompress with gunzip.

how.text: `gzip file` compresses the file to `file.gz` and **removes the original** unless `-k` (keep) is given. `gunzip file.gz` (or `gzip -d`) restores it. `-c` writes to stdout and leaves the file alone, which is how to compress in a pipeline. gzip handles one file; for many files use `tar -z`. `zcat file.gz` prints a compressed file without unpacking it, so `zcat log.gz | grep ERROR` works.

flags.d: Write to stdout, keep the input.

examples.desc: Compress and keep the original
Compress a stream
Search a compressed log without unpacking

blocks.name: shasum
blocks.sum: Compute or verify SHA checksums of files.

how.text: `shasum -a 256 file` prints a 64-hex-digit fingerprint and the file name. Publishers list these next to downloads so you can confirm the file is intact and unmodified. `shasum -c list.txt` reads lines of `checksum  name` and reports `OK` or `FAILED` per file. SHA-256 is the safe default; MD5 and SHA-1 are fine for catching accidents but not for security.

flags.d: Check files against a list of checksums.

examples.desc: Fingerprint a file
Record checksums for a folder, then verify later
Find duplicate files by content

gotchas: Compare the checksum from the publisher's page, not from the same page that served the file; a compromised server can change both.

blocks.name: md5
blocks.sum: Print the MD5 hash of files or strings (BSD tool; Linux calls it md5sum).

how.text: macOS ships `md5`, with output like `MD5 (file) = d41d8cd9...`, where Linux has `md5sum`. `-q` prints only the hash and `-s` hashes a string. MD5 is broken for security (collisions are easy) but still common for detecting accidental corruption.

examples.desc: Hash a file, hash only
Compare two files by hash
examples.code: [[ "$(md5 -q a.txt)" == "$(md5 -q b.txt)" ]] && echo same || echo different

blocks.name: ditto
blocks.sum: Copy directories and create or extract zip archives while preserving macOS metadata.
blocks.syntax: ditto [-c -k] [--keepParent] source destination      ditto -x -k archive.zip destination

how.text: `ditto src dst` copies a folder tree and keeps resource forks, extended attributes, ACLs and permissions, which makes it the right tool for copying `.app` bundles. Unlike `cp -R`, it merges into an existing destination rather than nesting. With `-c -k` it writes a zip the way Finder's "Compress" does (`--keepParent` keeps the top folder), and `-x -k` extracts one.

flags.d: Include the source folder itself in the archive.

examples.desc: Copy an app bundle exactly
Zip like Finder does
Archive and verify in one line

blocks.text: Permissions in depth

Every file and directory has an **owner**, a **group** and a set of **permission bits**. When a process tries to open a file, the kernel picks **one** class: if the process runs as the owner, the owner bits apply; otherwise, if it is in the file's group, the group bits; otherwise the "others" bits. Only the first matching class counts, so an owner with `---` cannot read their own file even if the group could.

head: Bit
On a **file**
On a **directory**
rows: create, delete and rename entries inside (needs `x` too)
**enter** it and access things by name (`cd`, `cat dir/file`)

blocks.text: The directory column explains puzzles. A directory with `r` but not `x` lets you see names but not open anything. A directory with `x` but not `r` lets you open a file whose name you already know but not list it. **Deleting a file needs write permission on its directory, not on the file.**
Three classes times three bits gives nine bits. Writing each class as one octal digit (r=4, w=2, x=1, added together) gives the usual short form:

head: Octal
Symbolic
Typical use
rows: ordinary file: owner writes, everyone reads
private file such as an SSH private key
program or directory everyone may use but only the owner edits

blocks.title: A symbolic chmod with two clauses

tokens.exp: then group and others (go): set (=) exactly read and execute, removing anything else; the comma separates clauses

blocks.text: Try the calculator above: set `755`, then toggle bits and watch the symbolic form and the `ls -l` string change together.
Special bits
A fourth leading octal digit (or an `s`/`t` in the `x` position) holds three special bits:

head: Bit
Octal
Effect
Where you see it
rows: the program runs as its **owner**, not as the user who started it
runs as the group; on a directory, new files inherit the directory's group
in a directory, only a file's owner (or root) can delete or rename it

blocks.text: A lowercase `s` or `t` means the underlying `x` is also set; an uppercase `S` or `T` means it is not, which is usually a mistake.
Owners, groups and who you are

blocks.name: id
blocks.sum: Print your user id, group id and every group you belong to.

how.text: `id` shows the numbers the kernel actually compares with file owners. On a Mac your first group is usually `staff` (20), and an administrator also belongs to `admin` (80), which is what lets you use `sudo`. `id -un` prints just the user name, `id -Gn` just the group names.

examples.desc: Who am I and what groups do I have?
Am I an administrator?
examples.code: id -Gn | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -qx admin && echo yes || echo no

blocks.name: whoami
blocks.sum: Print the name of the user running the shell.

how.text: `whoami` prints the effective user name. Run it after `sudo` to see `root`: `sudo whoami`. It is useful in scripts that must refuse to run as root.

examples.desc: Check
Refuse to run as root
examples.code: [[ "$(whoami)" == root ]] && { echo "do not run as root" >&2; exit 1; }

blocks.name: groups
blocks.sum: Print the groups a user belongs to.

how.text: `groups` prints group names for you or for a named user. Group membership is how several users share files: put a file in group `staff`, give the group write access, and every member can edit it.

examples.desc: Your groups
One group per line

blocks.name: chmod
blocks.sum: Change a file's permission bits, using octal numbers or symbolic expressions.

how.text: An **octal** mode sets all nine bits at once (`chmod 644 file`). A **symbolic** mode changes some and leaves the rest: `u`, `g`, `o`, `a` choose the class (user/owner, group, others, all), `+` adds, `-` removes, `=` sets exactly, followed by `r w x`. Several clauses are separated by commas: `chmod u=rwx,go=rx file`. Capital `X` adds execute only to directories and to files that already have execute, which is what you want with `-R`. You can only change files you own (or use `sudo`).

flags.d: Add execute for all classes allowed by the umask.
Add execute for the owner only.
Remove write from group and others.
Octal: owner read and write, nothing else.
macOS: add an ACL entry (`chmod +a "group:staff allow read" file`).

examples.desc: Make a script runnable
Make a key private
Files 644 and directories 755 across a tree
examples.code: find {{dir}} -type f -exec chmod 644 {} + && find {{dir}} -type d -exec chmod 755 {} +

examples.desc: Find world-writable files in a folder

anat.exp: (a second clause, joined with a comma) remove write from group and others

gotchas: `chmod -R 777` makes everything writable by every account and executable, and hides real problems. It is almost never the fix. Find who needs access and grant that.
After `chmod +x`, `./script.zsh` works but plain `script.zsh` does not unless its folder is on your `PATH`: the shell does not search `.`.

blocks.name: chown
blocks.sum: Change the owner and, optionally, the group of files.

how.text: Only root can give a file to another user, so `chown` normally runs under `sudo`. The usual real-world use on a Mac is repairing ownership after something was run as root: files in your home folder that became `root`-owned and now give `Permission denied` on write. `-R` recurses; be sure of the path before using it.

flags.d: Change a symbolic link itself, not its target.

examples.desc: Take back a folder that root created
Find files in your lab that you do not own

gotchas: `sudo chown -R` on the wrong path, such as `/` or `/usr`, can break the system. Check the path with `ls -ld` first, and keep it to folders under your home.

blocks.name: chgrp
blocks.sum: Change the group of files.

how.text: `chgrp group file` sets the group owner, which you may do for groups you belong to. It is the group-only form of `chown :group`.

examples.desc: Hand a folder to the staff group

blocks.name: umask
blocks.sum: Show or set the bits removed from the permissions of newly created files.

how.text: New files start at `666` (no execute) and new directories at `777`; the **umask** is subtracted bit by bit. The macOS default `022` therefore yields files `644` and directories `755`. A stricter `077` makes new files private (`600`/`700`). It applies to the current shell and its children, so put a chosen value in `~/.zshrc`.

flags.d: Print the mask in symbolic form (`u=rwx,g=rx,o=rx`).

examples.desc: See the current mask
Test a stricter mask in a subshell
Compare the result of two masks
examples.code: (umask 022; touch a.txt) && (umask 077; touch b.txt) && ls -l a.txt b.txt

blocks.name: sudo
blocks.sum: Run one command as another user, normally root, after authenticating.

how.text: `sudo` checks that your account is allowed (administrators are, through the `admin` group), asks for **your own** password (nothing appears as you type it), and runs the command with root's privileges. The authentication is cached for a few minutes. `sudo -k` forgets it immediately, `-l` lists what you may run, `-u user` runs as someone else. A redirection such as `sudo echo x > /etc/file` does **not** work, because the shell opens the file as you before `sudo` starts; use `echo x | sudo tee /etc/file`.

flags.d: Run as USER instead of root.
List the commands you are allowed to run.
Refresh the cached credentials without running a command.

examples.desc: Edit a root-owned file safely, with tee
List a folder only root may read
Check what a root-only tool prints, without a shell as root

gotchas: macOS 14 and later can use Touch ID for `sudo` by enabling `pam_tid.so` in `/etc/pam.d/sudo_local`; edit it carefully and keep another terminal open while testing.

blocks.text: Root ignores permission bits. A mistyped path under `sudo rm` or `sudo chown -R` can wreck the system, and a program run with `sudo` writes root-owned files into your home folder that later fail with `Permission denied` for you. Run the command without `sudo` first: the error message usually shows what you need. Read any `curl ... | sudo sh` instructions in full before running them.
Extra macOS layers
Classic permissions are only the first check on a Mac. When you get an error that `chmod` cannot explain, look at these:

items.text: **Extended attributes.** An `@` after the permissions in `ls -l` means the file carries xattrs. `ls -l@` or `xattr -l file` lists them. The best known is `com.apple.quarantine`, which the browser attaches to downloads.

**ACLs.** A `+` after the permissions means an access control list adds rules beyond the nine bits. `ls -le` shows them. Folders such as `~/Desktop` have a rule denying delete (`group:everyone deny delete`).
**File flags.** `ls -lO` shows flags such as `hidden`, `uchg` (user immutable: even the owner gets `Operation not permitted` until `chflags nouchg file`) and `restricted` (protected by SIP).

**System Integrity Protection (SIP).** Protects `/System`, `/usr` (except `/usr/local`), `/bin` and `/sbin` even from root. Check it with `csrutil status`. You will see `Operation not permitted` where `sudo` would normally work. Do not turn SIP off to work around a problem.

**Privacy permissions (TCC).** Even your own folders such as `~/Documents`, `~/Desktop`, `~/Downloads`, Mail data and Safari data are guarded per application. If Terminal prints `Operation not permitted` reading them, grant Terminal access under System Settings, Privacy & Security, Full Disk Access (or Files and Folders), then restart Terminal.

blocks.name: xattr
blocks.sum: List, read and delete extended attributes, including the Gatekeeper quarantine flag.

how.text: Extended attributes are named blobs of metadata attached to a file. When a browser, Mail or AirDrop delivers a file, macOS adds `com.apple.quarantine`; the first time you open the file, Gatekeeper checks the app and shows a "downloaded from the Internet" prompt. `xattr -l file` lists the attributes, `-p name` prints one, `-d name` deletes one, `-c` clears all, and `-r` recurses. Files fetched with `curl` or built locally are normally not quarantined.

examples.desc: Look at what a download carries
Remove the quarantine flag from an app you trust
Which items in Downloads are quarantined?
examples.code: for f in ~/Downloads/*(N); do xattr -p com.apple.quarantine "$f" > /dev/null 2>&1 && echo "$f"; done

gotchas: Removing quarantine disables a macOS safety check for that file. Do it only for software whose source you trust and have verified, for example with `shasum -a 256`.

blocks.title: Permission denied versus Operation not permitted

blocks.text: `Permission denied` means the classic bits, ownership or ACLs refuse you: inspect with `ls -ld`, `id` and fix with `chmod` or `chown`. `Operation not permitted` means something stronger said no: SIP, a file flag, or a privacy rule, and `sudo` will not help. The two messages point at different fixes.
Recipes: files in pipelines
Everything in this chapter produces text or paths that feed the pipelines from [Streams, Redirection & Pipes](#pipes):

blocks.code:
$ cd ~/lab
$ find . -type f | wc -l
      14
$ find . -name '*.log' -exec wc -l {} + | sort -rn | head -3
     143 total
     120 ./access.log
      15 ./ping.log
$ ls -lS data | head -3
total 40
-rw-r--r--  1 learner  staff  155 Sep 14 10:22 gamma.log
-rw-r--r--  1 learner  staff  149 Sep 14 10:22 delta.log
$ du -sh data
24K	data

blocks.title: Find, then act safely on every hit

tokens.exp: keep names ending in .tmp (quoted for the shell)
write names separated by NUL bytes instead of newlines
read NUL-separated names and pass them as arguments
the command to run on them, verbosely

blocks.text: More patterns worth typing once:

blocks.code:
# the five biggest files under a folder, size in bytes (column 5)
find ~/lab -type f -exec ls -l {} + | sort -k5 -rn | head -5

# directory sizes, largest last
du -sh ~/lab/* | sort -h

# the same with zsh only: five largest regular files, recursively
print -l ~/lab/**/*(.OL[1,5])

# which files changed in the last hour
find ~/lab -type f -mmin -60

# every file extension and how many of each
find ~/lab -type f | awk -F. 'NF>1 {print $NF}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

blocks.text: Common mistakes

items.text: **Unquoted `-name *.log`.** The shell expands it first. Quote the pattern.
**`mv file dir` with a missing `dir`** silently renames the file. Add a trailing slash.
**Deleting without looking.** Run the `ls` or `find -print` first.
**`sudo` as a first resort.** It creates root-owned files in your home that break later steps.
**`chmod 777`.** Grants everyone everything and fixes nothing.
**Forgetting the directory's `x` bit.** A file with perfect permissions is unreachable inside a directory without `x`.
**Extracting a tarball blindly.** List with `tar -tzf` first; some archives have no top-level folder and spill into the current directory.
**Trusting a downloaded file.** Compare checksums from the publisher's own site.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Reorganize a copy with globs

task.text: Make a working copy `~/lab/data-work` of `~/lab/data` (leave the original alone). Inside the copy, create the folders `logs`, `text` and `reports`, then move every `.log` file into `logs`, every `.txt` file into `text` and every `.csv` file into `reports`. Show the result as a tree or listing.

hints: `cp -R` makes the copy. A brace expansion such as `{logs,text,reports}` creates the three folders at once.
Globs like `*.log` match only inside the current directory, so `cd` into the copy first. Keep `archive` where it is.
blocks.solution:
cp -R ~/lab/data ~/lab/data-work
cd ~/lab/data-work
mkdir -p {logs,text,reports}
mv *.log logs/
mv *.txt text/
mv *.csv reports/
ls -R

why.text: Brace expansion creates the folders, and globs expand to the matching names before `mv` runs, so one command moves many files. The trailing slash on the destination makes a missing folder an error rather than a rename.

blocks.title: Find the five largest files

task.text: List the five largest regular files anywhere under `~/lab` with their sizes in bytes, largest first. Do it once with `find` and a pipeline, and once with a single zsh glob using qualifiers.

hints: `find ... -exec wc -c {} +` prints sizes and a `total` line; filter that line out.
In zsh, `OL` orders by size descending and `[1,5]` keeps five results.
blocks.solution:
find ~/lab -type f -exec wc -c {} + | grep -v ' total$' | sort -rn | head -5
print -l ~/lab/**/*(.OL[1,5])

why.text: `wc -c` is a portable way to get sizes that sorts numerically. The glob qualifier version does the finding, ordering and truncation in one expression, but works only in zsh.

blocks.title: Make a script executable

task.text: In `~/lab/scratch` (create it), write a two-line zsh script `hello.zsh` that prints `hello from $PWD`. Run it with `./hello.zsh` and read the error. Fix it with `chmod`, run it again, and check its permissions with `ls -l` and `stat -f '%Lp'`.

hints: The first run fails with `permission denied` because new files are not executable (`644`).
`chmod u+x hello.zsh` adds execute for you only.
blocks.solution:
mkdir -p ~/lab/scratch && cd ~/lab/scratch
printf '#!/bin/zsh\necho "hello from $PWD"\n' > hello.zsh
./hello.zsh
chmod u+x hello.zsh
./hello.zsh
ls -l hello.zsh; stat -f '%Lp' hello.zsh

why.text: The kernel refuses to execute a file without an `x` bit (shell exit status 126). `u+x` turns on exactly one bit. The permissions went from `644` to `744`.

blocks.title: Recover from Permission denied

task.text: Break it on purpose, then fix it. Create `~/lab/locked/secret.txt` and remove all permissions from the folder with `chmod 000 ~/lab/locked`. Try to `cat` the file and `ls` the folder. Diagnose with `ls -ld`, work out which bit is missing, and restore access with the **smallest** change that lets you read the file and list the folder.

hints: Use `ls -ld ~/lab/locked` to see the mode, and think about what `r` and `x` each give you on a directory.
You need `x` to open the file inside and `r` to list the folder. As the owner, `u+rx` is enough.
blocks.solution:
mkdir -p ~/lab/locked && echo secret > ~/lab/locked/secret.txt
chmod 000 ~/lab/locked
cat ~/lab/locked/secret.txt
ls ~/lab/locked
ls -ld ~/lab/locked
chmod u+rx ~/lab/locked
cat ~/lab/locked/secret.txt

why.text: Both commands fail because the directory has no `x` (cannot enter) and no `r` (cannot list). `ls -ld` shows `d---------`. Granting only the owner `r` and `x` fixes it without exposing the folder to others, unlike `chmod -R 777`.

blocks.title: Archive, verify, restore

task.text: Pack `~/lab/data` into `data.tgz` in `~/lab/scratch`, list the archive, record its SHA-256 in `data.tgz.sha256`, extract it into a new folder `~/lab/scratch/restore`, and prove with `diff -r` that the restored copy equals the original.

hints: Use `-C ~/lab` so the archive holds relative paths like `data/alpha.txt`.
`diff -r original restored` prints nothing when the trees are identical.
blocks.solution:
cd ~/lab/scratch
tar -czf data.tgz -C ~/lab data
tar -tzf data.tgz
shasum -a 256 data.tgz > data.tgz.sha256
mkdir -p restore && tar -xzf data.tgz -C restore
diff -r ~/lab/data restore/data && echo identical

why.text: `-C` keeps archive paths relative, so extraction cannot overwrite anything outside `restore`. A checksum proves the archive file itself was not altered, and `diff -r` proves the contents match.

blocks.title: Permissions in code

task.text: Write `symbolic(mode)` that takes an integer mode such as `0o755` and returns the 9-character permission string as `ls -l` shows it (`rwxr-xr-x`). Handle the special bits: setuid shows `s` (or `S` if the owner has no execute), setgid shows `s`/`S` in the group triple, and sticky shows `t`/`T` in the others triple.

hints: Shift the mode right by 6, 3 and 0 and mask with 7 to get the owner, group and other digits.
After building the nine characters, replace the `x` positions (indexes 2, 5, 8) according to the special bits.

why.text: This is exactly what `ls -l` does. Octal digits are three bits each, so shifts and masks pull them apart, and the special bits live in the fourth digit. It is the same bit arithmetic as subnet masks in [Addressing & Subnetting](#addressing).

blocks.check:
assert symbolic(0o755) == "rwxr-xr-x", "755 should be rwxr-xr-x"
assert symbolic(0o644) == "rw-r--r--", "644 should be rw-r--r--"
assert symbolic(0o600) == "rw-------", "600 should be rw-------"
assert symbolic(0o4755) == "rwsr-xr-x", "4755 is setuid with owner execute: rwsr-xr-x"
assert symbolic(0o1777) == "rwxrwxrwt", "1777 is sticky: rwxrwxrwt"
assert symbolic(0o4644) == "rwSr--r--", "setuid without owner execute shows S"
assert symbolic(0o2755) == "rwxr-sr-x", "setgid with group execute shows s in the group triple"

questions.q: A directory has mode `r--r--r--`. As its owner, what can you do?

options.text: List its files and open them
List the file names but not open files or enter it

questions.why: Without `x` on a directory you cannot enter it or access things inside by name. With only `r` you can read the names with `ls`, but `cd` and opening files fail. Creating files needs `w` and `x`.
6 is rw- for the owner, 4 is r-- for the group, 0 is --- for others.

questions.q: Which command lists the five most recently modified entries?
questions.why: `-t` sorts by modification time, newest first. `-S` sorts by size and `-r` only reverses the current order.

questions.q: Why does `sudo echo "x" > /etc/hosts` fail with permission denied?

options.text: echo does not work with sudo
The redirection is performed by your shell as you, before sudo starts
sudo only works for programs, not for files

questions.why: The shell opens the output file as you. Use `echo x | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts` so a root process opens it.

questions.q: Which `find` option, placed correctly, deletes matching files?
questions.why: `-delete` removes each match. Always run the same `find` with `-print` first and read the list.

questions.q: A message says `Operation not permitted` while you are root. What is the likely cause?

options.text: The file is read-only for others
System Integrity Protection, a file flag, or a privacy (TCC) rule
A typo in the file name

questions.why: Classic permission problems produce `Permission denied`. `Operation not permitted` points to SIP, flags like `uchg`, or macOS privacy protections, which `chmod` and `sudo` do not override.

blocks.text: You will make a small reproducible backup of the lab: select what to keep, pack it with a dated name, fingerprint it, and prove it restores, with permissions that suit a backup.
Step 1: Decide what goes in

blocks.code:
cd ~/lab
find . -type f ! -name '.DS_Store' | sort | head -20
du -sh .

blocks.text: Step 2: Create the dated archive
`--exclude './backups'` stops the backup from containing itself.
Step 3: Fingerprint and protect it

blocks.code:
cd ~/lab/backups
shasum -a 256 lab-$stamp.tgz > lab-$stamp.tgz.sha256
chmod 400 lab-$stamp.tgz lab-$stamp.tgz.sha256
ls -l

blocks.text: Read-only (`400`) is a guard against accidental overwrite; remove it with `chmod u+w` when you want to delete old backups.
Step 4: Verify and restore

blocks.code:
shasum -c lab-$stamp.tgz.sha256
rm -rf /tmp/lab-restore && mkdir -p /tmp/lab-restore
tar -xzf lab-$stamp.tgz -C /tmp/lab-restore
diff -r --exclude backups ~/lab /tmp/lab-restore && echo "restore matches"

blocks.text: Put the four steps into a `backup.zsh` script with `setopt pipefail`, take the source folder as an argument, and keep only the newest five archives with `ls -t lab-*.tgz | tail -n +6 | xargs rm -f`. You will do this properly in [Scripting](#scripting).
Next: [Text-processing toolkit](#text) gives you grep, sed, awk and friends for reshaping the text that all these commands produce.

terms.def: The text that names a file's location, such as /Users/learner/lab/access.log
A path that starts at the root directory (/), meaning the same everywhere
A path interpreted from the current working directory
The filesystem record that stores a file's metadata and data location; names are entries that point to inodes
A small file holding a path to another file or directory (a shortcut)
A second directory entry pointing to the same inode as another name
The nine read/write/execute flags for owner, group and others stored with each file
Permissions written as three or four digits, each summing r=4, w=2, x=1
The mask of permission bits removed from newly created files and directories
A permission bit that makes a program run with its owner's privileges instead of the caller's
A directory bit that lets only a file's owner (or root) delete or rename files inside
Access control list: extra per-user or per-group permission rules beyond the basic nine bits
An extended attribute: named metadata attached to a file, such as com.apple.quarantine
The attribute macOS puts on downloaded files so Gatekeeper checks them on first open
System Integrity Protection: macOS protection that stops even root from modifying system locations
A short fingerprint of data computed with a hash function; it changes if the data changes
